title: Given an N by N matrix where each row and each column is sorted in ascending order, find the Kth smallest element in the matrix. Explain the K-way Merge heap technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix (Row and Column Sorted Matrix)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix treats each row as a sorted list and applies early-stopped K-way Merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each row, pop K times, and after each pop push the next element in that same row. The Kth popped value is the answer, costing K log N time and N space for an N by N matrix.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps a grid of fees where each row and column rises. To find the Kth cheapest fee, a clerk starts with the leftmost fee of every row on a small tray, pops the cheapest, and slides one step right in that same row to replace it. After K pops the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Rows are sorted lists; run K-way Merge across rows and stop at the Kth pop.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix treats each row as a sorted list and applies early-stopped K-way Merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each row, pop K times, and after each pop push the next element in that same row. The Kth popped value is the answer, costing K log N time and N space for an N by N matrix.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps a grid of fees where each row and column rises. To find the Kth cheapest fee, a clerk starts with the leftmost fee of every row on a small tray, pops the cheapest, and slides one step right in that same row to replace it. After K pops the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.

**One line to remember:** Rows are sorted lists; run K-way Merge across rows and stop at the Kth pop.

sections.s2_technical:
Each row is already ascending, so the matrix is really N sorted rows. The heap entry stores the value, the row, and the column: `{value, row, col}`. We seed with column zero of each row, then pop K times. After popping `{v, r, c}` we push `{matrix[r][c+1], r, c+1}` if the column plus one is still in range.

A seed looks like `pq.add(new int[]{matrix[r][0], r, 0})` for each row r. Senior nuance: we only need to seed as many rows as K at most, but seeding all N rows is simple and still N space; the heap size stays bounded by N because each row contributes one live candidate. The column-sorted property is not needed for correctness here, only the row-sorted property, which is a point interviewers like to probe.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores a fee matrix where moving right along a row or down a column only increases the fee, and the product team needs the Kth smallest fee to set a tier boundary. Scanning and sorting every cell wastes the built-in ordering. This is exactly how Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix works: it advances a row-wise K-way merge only K steps.

The code defines a `FeeMatrixService` exposing `kthSmallest(matrix, k)` returning the Kth smallest cell value. A `Demo` builds a small sorted matrix and logs the Kth smallest fee.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a three by three matrix with rows 2,6,8 then 3,7,10 then 5,8,11. We want the fifth smallest fee.

Step 1 — We seed the heap with the first column of each row, which is 2, 3, and 5. The heap holds three entries, one per row.

Step 2 — Pop one: 2 from row zero. Push the next in that row, 6. Count one. Heap holds 6, 3, 5.

Step 3 — Pop two: 3 from row one. Push 7. Count two. Heap holds 6, 7, 5.

Step 4 — Pop three: 5 from row two. Push 8. Count three. Heap holds 6, 7, 8.

Step 5 — Pop four: 6 from row zero, push 8, count four. Pop five: 7 from row one, count reaches five and we stop. The fifth smallest fee is 7, shown below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:49:02 PM com.bank.matrix.service.FeeMatrixService kthSmallest
INFO: Kth smallest (k=5) = 7
Oct 27, 2026 8:49:02 PM com.bank.matrix.FeeMatrixApplication main
INFO: The 5th smallest fee is Rs.7
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: row-sorted matrix, k = 5
    row0: 2 6 8
    row1: 3 7 10
    row2: 5 8 11
    │
    ▼
  Seed heap with column 0 of each row: {2,3,5}
    │
    ▼
  Pop k times, push next-in-row each time
    │ pop 2 → push 6   count 1
    │ pop 3 → push 7   count 2
    │ pop 5 → push 8   count 3
    │ pop 6 → push 8   count 4
    │ pop 7 → STOP     count 5 ← answer
    ▼
  Output: 5th smallest = 7
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix is a K-way Merge problem once I notice that each row is already a sorted list. I seed a min-heap with the first element of each row, carrying the value along with its row and column so I can fetch the next element in that row, then I pop K times and after every pop I push the next cell to the right in the same row. The value of the Kth pop is the Kth smallest in the whole matrix.

What I highlight to an interviewer is that only the row-sorted property is required for this approach to be correct; the column-sorted property is a nice bonus the problem gives but my heap merge does not depend on it. The heap holds at most N candidates, one per row, so K pops cost K log N and the space is N. I also seed only up to K rows because no element below row K can be among the first K smallest.

At the National Bank of India I used this on a fee grid where moving right or down only increased the fee, and the product team needed the Kth smallest fee to set a pricing tier boundary. Rather than flattening and sorting every cell, I ran a row-wise K-way merge and stopped at the Kth removal. Explaining that rows are sorted lists, that the column order is not needed for this method, and that the cost is K log N is what shows an interviewer I see the K-way Merge pattern hidden inside a matrix question.
